chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Ja'far ibn Uthman, from Sama'a, from Abi Basir, and Wuhayb ibn Hafs, from Abi Basir, from Abi Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
Allah has two kinds of knowledge: a hidden and stored-up knowledge, which He alone knows, from that comes Bada'; and a knowledge which He taught His angels, messengers, and prophets, so we know it.
ai.seo_question: What are the two types of divine knowledge in Shia theology and how does Bada' relate to them?
ai.summary: This hadith establishes the theological foundation for Bada' by distinguishing between Allah's absolute, exclusive knowledge (where change occurs) and the contingent knowledge granted to the divine hierarchy. In Shia scholarship, this hierarchy culminates in the Imams, who possess the revealed knowledge of the prophets, thereby serving as the ultimate authorities on divine decree and its manifestations in history. This distinction resolves the apparent paradox of God's omniscience with His ability to alter decrees based on new conditions.
